newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Broker Petercam sees 2.0 pct Belgian GDP growth 97.
newsitem.headline: Broker Petercam sees 2.0 pct Belgian GDP growth 97.

text.p: Belgian gross domestic product should grow 2.0 percent in 1997, with the economic recovery more solidly based than it was in 1994 but losing momentum in the second half, Belgian brokerage Petercam said on Monday.

"The recovery is not built on loose ground as in 1994. Yet it is not founded on rock either...We think it is built on still wet concrete that has to harden further to become solid," Petercam said in its latest bi-monthly research pamphlet.

Petercam said its 2.0 percent growth forecast could be shifted upwards slighty, but could surpass 2.5 percent only if quick and decisive steps were taken to solving structural European problems of competitiveness.
"Still, what does not come in 1997 can fuel a growth outbreak in the 'Euro-transition years' from 1998 onwards," it added. The consensus forecast for 1997 growth is 2.2 percent.
Earlier this month the Belgian National Bank upped its growth forecast for 1996 by 0.2 percentage point to 1.4 percent.
Petercam said it had been negative on growth prospects for 1996, for reasons which had now turned more favourable.

These included the fact core European currencies were currently less over-valued than last year, Belgian interest rates had fallen to historic lows and fiscal policy was now relatively neutral for economic growth.

Consumers' confidence had deteriorated too far, with the gap between their real financial position and actual spending widening to deep recessionary levels. This created pent up demand and so consumption potential for the years ahead.

Also, the balance of power was shifting towards the corporate sector again, as the government re-awakened to the sector's role as a factor for growth and future welfare and responded with "corporate conscious" measures.
Petercam forecast 1997 inflation at 2.1 percent - unchanged from 1996 - saying it was in a downward trend but had been kept up by tax increases and a rise in petrol prices.
